newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's biggest industrial firm sees profit, stock soars.
newsitem.headline: France's biggest industrial firm sees profit, stock soars.

text.p: Alcatel Alsthom, France's biggest industrial company, Thursday forecast stronger-than-expected profits for 1996 after a huge loss in 1995, sending its stock soaring and the Paris market's leading index to a record high.

The electrical engineering company said it expected to post net income of 2.5 billion francs ($452 million) after a 25.6 billion franc ($4.6 billion) loss in 1995 -- the biggest ever by a French company -- when it had to pay for massive restucturing to adapt to new competition.
Analysts had expected Alcatel to show a 1996 profit closer to 1.4 billion francs ($253 million). Final results are due in March.

"After taking into account exceptional items, and in particular capital gains resulting from the non-strategic asset disposal programme, the group's 1996 net income should amount to approximately 2.5 billion (francs)," Alcatel said in a statement.
Sales came in at 162.0 billion francs ($29.3 billion), little changed from 1995, and orders rose 8 percent, reflecting a pick-up in business activity.
Alcatel stock jumped 15.5 percent to a year high of 523 francs ($94.55), helping the blue-chip CAC-40 share index up 38.05 points to a record 2,503.06.
"The share has been massacred on the bourse, today it is catching up," one analyst said.
A recovery in the telecommunications sector, where Alcatel is a top equipment supplier, helped push operating earnings up sharply last year.
Its undersea cable division also had rebounded late last year.
Alcatel said its 1996 performance underscored its recovery plans and confirmed the company's target of reaching a "satisfactory level of profitability in 1998."
The 1996 profit would be the first for chairman Serge Tchuruk since he took over an ailing giant with activities as diverse as telecommunications and high-speed trains in 1995.
The group had fallen on hard times during explosive growth in mobile telecommunications and austerity drives by telephone companies facing new competition and deregulation after 1998.
Tchuruk slimmed down management, reorganized the company along product lines and initiated cost cuts and asset sales.

The 1995 loss, France's worst this century, was almost entirely due to exceptional charges of 23.9 billion francs ($4.3 billion) to pay for restructuring. The company cut about 20,000 jobs, mainly in Europe, from 191,000 at year-end 1995.
Last September, Alcatel said it had cut its first-half losses sharply and predicted a profit for 1996.
